# Use Case

## Background

It is hard to talk about the history of the **Philadelphia Chinatown** without the construction of **I-676**, also known as the **Vine Street Expressway** which bisected the neighborhood. Although the highway serves as a significant thoroughfare through Center City Philadelphia, the indispensable repercussions on the adjacent neighborhoods still lingers today. Consequences of the highway such as demolition of buildings, pedestrian safety threats, traffic congestion, as well as noise and air pollution has been harming Chinatown and its surrounding neighborhoods over the past decades and are yet to be addressed.

In the last couple of years, [City of Philadelphia Office of Transportation and Infrastructure Systems (OTIS)](https://www.phila.gov/departments/office-of-transportation-and-infrastructure-systems/) brought forth the plan to cap sections of the expressway to address its historical harms to the Chinatown region. This project, titled **the Chinatown Stitch project**, is aimed to create a safe and equitable green space for the public that would reconnect areas north and south to the Vine Street expressway. Receiving funds from the US department of Transportation through the [Bipartisan Infrastructure Law](https://www.transit.dot.gov/IIJA), the construction of phase one the Chinatown Stitch will start in 2027 and is expected to be completed in early 2030.

This purpose of this study is to help OTIS **understand how the property values in Philadelphia's Chinatown region will change after the implementation of the Chinatown Stitch**. The first part of the study will focus on the effects of highways on property sales prices in Philadelphia and more specifically in our study area. We also include key findings from our qualitative research on highway effects and caps in other cities. Prices will then be estimated using **a predictive model** which we validate with real data. We then use this model to predict how property price will change in **three alternate futures**: Scenario 0 - business as usual, without the implementation of the Chinatown Stitch; Scenario 1 - implementation of the Chinatown Stitch; and Scenario 2 - implementation of the Chinatown Stitch and the addition of more commercial and residential transformations in our study area.

We were tasked with building a [data-driven story map](https://yixuanzhou123.github.io/Practicum_Storymap/introduction.html) to explain possible impacts of the **Chinatown Stitch** to residents of neighborhoods surrounding the project area (we will define this area shortly). This report includes **all** of the analysis that we conducted, while the story map highlights what we deemed most pressing and important to residents. 

A note to the reader: please click on "SHOW" to see the code behind all of our analyses. Some code chunks may have code commented out. This usually signifies that we have already run the code chunks and have saved the data on our [Github repository](https://github.com/Bluebird-hi/Chinatown-Practicum/tree/main). We call in the pre-saved data, but provide our code for transparency.

Three study areas are used in our report and they are as follows. 

-   **Philadelphia:** We explore properties throughout the city of Philadelphia to conduct the first step of our highway analysis.
-   **Main study area (10 block groups):** Incorporating block groups from Chinatown, Callowhill, Logan Square, Center City East, Old City, and West Poplar, this study area is used to investigate the relationship between I-676 and property sales price. This is the main study area we use for our predictive model as well.
-   **North and South Split:** We split our main study area into areas [North]{style="color: #eb5600;"} and [South]{style="color: #1a9988;"} of I-676 (which we refer to as Callowhill and Chinatown, respectively, for simplicity). This allows us to see how the highway effect is felt differently across the highway.

With all the green space that the Chinatown Stitch will provide, we treat the area as a **park**, providing residents and visitors not only a natural and inviting space, but increasing opportunities for social interaction or even rest from the buzzing city life. In addition, OTIS is designing the Chinatown Stitch with phase two of the **Rail Park** (in the [north (Callowhill)]{style="color: #eb5600;"}) in mind. There are many existing **cultural and commercial resources** to the [south (Chinatown)]{style="color: #1a9988;"} of the expressway, and [OTIS's community surveys](https://www.phila.gov/media/20231219094529/Chinatown-Stitch-Vision-Report-December-2023.pdf) have found that residents would like to see some commercial development in addition to a community garden and picnic area on the highway cap as well.

## Methodology

With the goal of **a data-driven story map**, our methodology is structured around constructing **a robust model construction process**. By incorporating illustrative data visualizations throughout our data analysis, the story map features engaging maps and compelling narratives to guide residents through the very complex relationship between highways and property prices.

![](Final%20R%20Markdown/Images/methodology.png)

To substantiate our quantitative investigation of how property value may react to the implementation of the Chinatown Stitch, a thorough **qualitative analysis** was undertaken. First, we conducted a literature review on the effects of highways in urban areas, specifically focusing on how proximity to highways influences home values, heavily leaning on the works of [Dr. Jeffrey Lin](https://www.philadelphiafed.org/our-people/jeffrey-lin), an economist from the Philadelphia Federal Reserve Bank. 

In addition, we conducted a **series of interviews** with experts with an exhaustive understanding of the **highway effects** on property prices (Dr. Lin), **Philadelphia Chinatown** and other Chinatowns across the country ([Dr. Domenic Vitiello](https://www.design.upenn.edu/people/domenic-vitiello)), and **design perspectives** that landscape architects consider when working on projects like the Chinatown Stitch ([Dr. Yadan Luo](https://www.design.upenn.edu/people/yadan-luo)). These interviews provided us with an interdisciplinary perspectives on the potential impacts of the Chinatown Stitch on local communities. 

We also explored **other completed highway capping projects** across the United States as case studies to hypothesize how the Chinatown Stitch Project may impact the social, environmental, and economical nature of the Philadelphia Chinatown.

# Exploratory Data Analysis
## Data Wrangling
### Data Sources
The core dataset of this project consists of parcel-level property records from [Philadelphia Properties and Assessment History](https://opendataphilly.org/datasets/philadelphia-properties-and-assessment-history/), which form the foundation for a quantitative analysis of the spatial effects of the I-676 highway. The analysis focuses on historical sale prices, property characteristics, and spatial location of parcels within Chinatown and adjacent neighborhoods. These data are used to simulate and visualize planning scenarios following the Chinatown Stitch intervention, enabling the community to better understand how property sale prices may shift under different policy changes.

### Property Data  
Our primary variable of interest, **property price**, is sourced from the [Philadelphia Properties and Assessment History](https://opendataphilly.org/datasets/philadelphia-properties-and-assessment-history/) dataset available on Open Data Philly. This dataset includes variables such as `sale_price`, number of bedrooms, parcel number, and property condition. To prepare the data for analysis, we apply the following preprocessing steps related to sale date, inflation adjustment, geographic transformation, and handling of missing values:

+ **Sale Date (Philadelphia Focus)**: To ensure price comparability, we limit our analysis to properties sold **between 2020 and 2024** within Philadelphia.

+ **Inflation Adjustment**: Sale prices are adjusted for inflation using the **Consumer Price Index (CPI)**, normalized to December 2024 values.

+ **Price Range Filtering**: We begin by removing records with **implausibly low sale prices (below $100)**. Then, to reduce the influence of outliers and enhance generalizability, we **trim both the bottom and top 5%** of the price distribution.

+ **Geographic Transformation**: Since spatial proximity to highways and other features influences property values, we reproject coordinates to **NAD83 / Pennsylvania South (EPSG: 2272)** for accurate spatial analysis.

+ **Missing Data Imputation**: Missing values for **zoning**, **central air**, and **year built** are filled using current property characteristics where available.

```{r property wrangling, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#### clean data for city wise - sale price
colnames(cpi_data) <- c("half1", "half2", "cpi_date")
cpi_long <- cpi_data %>%
  mutate(
    Jan = `half1`, Feb = `half1`, Mar = `half1`, Apr = `half1`, May = `half1`, Jun = `half1`,
    Jul = `half2`, Aug = `half2`, Sep = `half2`, Oct = `half2`, Nov = `half2`, Dec = `half2`
  ) %>%
  select(-half1, -half2) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -cpi_date, names_to = "Month", values_to = "CPI") %>%
  mutate(
    Month = match(Month, month.abb),
    date = as.Date(paste(cpi_date, Month, "01", sep = "-"))  
  ) %>%
  select(date, CPI)

property_philly <-property%>%
  mutate(sale_date = as.Date(sale_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d")) %>%
  filter(sale_date >= as.Date("2020-01-01") & sale_date <= as.Date("2024-12-31"))%>%
  filter(!is.na(sale_price), !is.na(total_livable_area))%>%
  mutate(
    sale_month = floor_date(sale_date, "month"))%>%
  left_join(cpi_long, by = c("sale_month" = "date"))%>%
  mutate(CPI = as.numeric(CPI))%>%
  mutate(adj_sale_price = sale_price * (340.331/CPI))%>%
  select(-sale_month, -recording_date,  -other_building, 
         -assessment_date, -mailing_address_2, mailing_city_state, mailing_care_of)

#mean_price <- mean(property_philly$adj_sale_price, na.rm = TRUE)
#sd_price <- sd(property_philly$adj_sale_price, na.rm = TRUE)
#extreme_outlier <- mean_price + 5 * sd_price

  filter(adj_sale_price >= 100)

q_philly <- quantile(price_filtered_philly$adj_sale_price, probs = c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE)

property_philly2 <- property_philly %>%
  filter(adj_sale_price >= q_philly[1], adj_sale_price <= q_philly[2])

    Jul = `half2`, Aug = `half2`, Sep = `half2`, Oct = `half2`, Nov = `half2`, Dec = `half2`
  ) %>%
```

```{r POI, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, quiet=TRUE, results='hide', eval = FALSE}
# POI - restaurant-drink-dessert
api_key <- "AIzaSyCa-yuy1Y3n07URlR2HHg6dp_cIEouv9hs"

all_responses <- list()

for (pt_idx in seq_len(nrow(coords))) {
  location <- coords[pt_idx, c(2,1)]  # lat, lng
  cat(" Querying center point", pt_idx, "at", paste(location, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  
  for (ptype in place_types) {
    for (kw in keywords) {
      Sys.sleep(5)  
      cat("🔎", kw, "in", ptype, "\n")

      response <- google_places(
        keyword = kw,
        location = location,
        radius = 2000,  
        place_type = ptype,
        key = api_key
      )

      if (is.null(response[["results"]]) || length(response[["results"]]) == 0) {
        cat("No results for:", kw, "in", ptype, "\n")
        next
      }

      page_token <- response$next_page_token
      results_list <- list(response[["results"]])
      i <- 1

      while (!is.null(page_token)) {
        Sys.sleep(10)
        response_next <- google_places(
          keyword = kw,
          location = location,
          radius = 2000,
          place_type = ptype,
          key = api_key,
          page_token = page_token
        )

        if (is.null(response_next[["results"]]) || length(response_next[["results"]]) == 0) break

        results_list[[i + 1]] <- response_next[["results"]]
        page_token <- response_next$next_page_token
        i <- i + 1
      }

      all_responses[[paste(kw, ptype, pt_idx, sep = "_")]] <- bind_rows(results_list) %>%
        filter(!is.na(place_id)) %>%
        distinct(place_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
    }
  }
}
```

### Neighborhood Context Data  
To capture the **neighborhood context** surrounding each parcel, we integrated multiple spatial datasets from [Open Data Philly](https://opendataphilly.org/datasets/), including parks, City Hall, transit stations (bus, metro and trolley), schools, hospitals, bodies of water, bike networks, and points-of-interest or POIs such as grocery stores and restaurants (via Google Places API). For each type of feature, we computed the distance to the nearest amenity for each property, generating a set of **spatial accessibility indicators** (i.e. distance to nearest restaurant, distance to nearest hospital, etc.). 

We further spatially joined each parcel to its corresponding **neighborhood name**, **land use** category, and **retail** environment data (low- or high-produce supply stores per 1,000 people, abbreviated to LPSS and HPSS, respectively) to enrich contextual attributes. **Crime rate** was calculated using historical crime records for Philadelphia. Specifically, we applied a k-nearest-neighbor (K-NN) approach (for values of k between 1 and 5) to derive the average distance to the nearest reported incidents for each property, reflecting localized safety levels.

These variables are essential indicators in our analysis and modeling, capturing how the **surrounding built and social environments may influence sale price** and responses to planning interventions.

```{r neighborhood_process}
calculate_nearest_distance <- function(set_points, other_layer) {
  nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(set_points, other_layer)
  st_distance(set_points, other_layer[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE) %>% as.numeric()
}

Luming_property <- property_studyarea %>%
  dplyr::select(objectid, geometry, sale_price) %>%
  rename(orig_objectid = objectid)

Luming_property <- Luming_property %>%
  mutate(distance_to_city_hall = st_distance(., city_hall) %>% as.numeric()) %>%
  mutate(
    distance_to_nearest_transit = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, transit),
    distance_to_nearest_hospital = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, hospital),
    distance_to_nearest_school = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, school),
    distance_to_nearest_park = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, park),
    distance_to_nearest_water = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, water),
    distance_to_nearest_bikelane = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, bike_network),
    distance_to_I676 = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, I_676)
  ) %>%
  st_join(nhood["NAME"], left = TRUE) %>%
  rename(nhoods_name = NAME) %>%
  st_join(landuse_rename["landuse"], left = TRUE) %>%
  st_join(retail[, c("LPSS_PER1000", "HPSS_PER1000")], left = TRUE)

Luming_property <- Luming_property %>% 
    mutate(
      crime_nn1 = nn_function(st_coordinates(Luming_property),
                              st_coordinates(phillyCrimes), k = 1),

      crime_nn2 = nn_function(st_coordinates(Luming_property),
                              st_coordinates(phillyCrimes), k = 2),

      crime_nn3 = nn_function(st_coordinates(Luming_property),
                              st_coordinates(phillyCrimes), k = 3),

      crime_nn4 = nn_function(st_coordinates(Luming_property),
                              st_coordinates(phillyCrimes), k = 4),
      
      crime_nn5 = nn_function(st_coordinates(Luming_property), 
                              st_coordinates(phillyCrimes), k = 5))
```

## Basic Geography of our Study Area

This land use map of our study area reveals several important aspects of the two neighborhoods divided by the Vine Street Expressway. [Callowhill (north of I-676)]{style="color: #eb5600;"} and [Chinatown (south of I-676)]{style="color: #1a9988;"} have starkly different land use patterns likely due to historical development reasons. The [Callowhill neighborhood]{style="color: #eb5600;"} has a higher portion of **industrial and vacant land** in contrast with the [Chinatown area]{style="color: #1a9988;"} that is predominantly occupied by **commercial business and mixed residential use land**.

The amenities map indicates that there is a **scarcity of green open space** within the boundary of our study area, highlighting the **limited access to recreational spaces** therefore making the implementation of the Chinatown Stitch even more demanding. There is also an obvious concentration of vacant land to the north of the expressway while the land south of the highway seems to be more actively utilized in comparison.

#### Sales Price Change

The following charts are retrieved from Zillow’s website as they indicate the Zillow Home Value Index (ZHVI) trends of property values in [Chinatown]{style="color: #1a9988;"}, Callowhill, as well as the entire city. The plot on the left suggests that [Chinatown]{style="color: #1a9988;"} has a stronger housing demand than the city average home value since 2017. As shown on the right panel, we observe that [Chinatown’s]{style="color: #1a9988;"} property values were substantially lower than [Callowhill’s]{style="color: #eb5600;"} values throughout the past eight years. Over the course of history, [Callowhill]{style="color: #eb5600;"} has transformed from a post-industrial area into a mixed-use residential area while [Chinatown]{style="color: #1a9988;"} remained to be more stable and maintained its urban and commercial character. 

We conclude that the difference in property price growth [north]{style="color: #eb5600;"} and [south]{style="color: #1a9988;"} of the highway may have been shaped by the construction of the Vine Street Expressway in addition to other historical large-scale development within the neighborhoods.

## Highway Effects Analysis

Before jumping into modeling, we first explored the relationship between **distance to highway** and **property prices**. 

### Findings from Qualitative Research

Our main takeaways from our literature review comes from the Lin and Brinkman paper which included the following findings [@LinHighwayEffects].

+ Freeways create both **accessibility benefits**, felt mostly in suburban neighborhoods, and **local disamenities** (noise, pollution, barrier effects) leading to reduced quality of life in central-city neighborhoods.
+ **One-third** of central-city population decline can be attributed to freeways disamenities, outweighing commuting and other benefits.
+ Targeted **policies to bury highways can provide net benefits**, especially ones that mitigate barrier effects created by highways.
+ Estimated lifetime **benefits of mitigation are comparable to costs**, suggesting some projects could pass a cost-benefit test.

With this in mind, we start our quantitative analyses at three different scales. First, we look at the effect of the four main highways in Philadelphia on properties within 500m of them. Then, we zoom into our study area and look at I-676 effects. Finally, we separate our study area into North and South to see how the highway effects are felt differently across different neighborhoods.

### Philadelphia Scale Analysis

We used property data from OPA Philadelphia that was cleaned the way we reported in the [Property Data] section.

Our **Philadelphia Scale Analysis** looks at properties (of all kinds, not limited to housing properties) within 500 m of Philadelphia's main highways -- [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"} on the East, [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"} on the West, [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"} in the North, and [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} through the city.

For each scale of analysis, we report highway effects by discussing the change in predicted property price from 50 to 150m away from the highway, conceptualizing a block to be roughly 100m. We report this in absolute value of change as well as percent change.

![](Final%20R%20Markdown/Images/reporting_highway_effect.png)

We saw the following trends in property prices

`r paste0(substr(nrow(prop500), 1, 2), ",", substr(nrow(prop500), 3, 5))` total properties were included in this analysis. We see that the distribution of log sale prices of properties within 500m of highways in Philadelphia generally follow a normal distribution.

Though there aren't as many properties near [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} (`r prop_count_676` properties) as there are near the other highways, they are most expensive group with a median property price of **`r paste0('$', substr(med_price_676, 1, 3), ',', substr(med_price_676, 4, 9))`**. 

Properties near [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"} and [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"} are among a similar range of prices with median property prices being **`r paste0('$', substr(med_price_i95, 1, 3), ',', substr(med_price_i95, 4, 9))`** and **`r paste0('$', substr(med_price_i76, 1, 3), ',', substr(med_price_i76, 4, 9))`**, respectively, though there are almost five times as many properties near [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"} compared to [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"} (`r paste0(substr(prop_count_i95,1,1), ",", substr(prop_count_i95, 2,4))` and `r paste0(substr(prop_count_i76,1,1), ",", substr(prop_count_i76, 2,4))` properties around [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"} and [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"}, respectively). 

Finally, there are many properties within 500m of [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"} (`r paste0(substr(prop_count_us1,1,1), ",", substr(prop_count_us1, 2,4))` properties), but the median property price was lowest compared to other highways at **`r paste0('$', substr(med_price_us1, 1, 3), ',', substr(med_price_us1, 4, 9))`**.

```{r prop500_faceted}
# models + beta coefficients
coef_us1 <- round(
  summary(
    lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway,
       data = prop500 %>% 
         filter(grepl("US", closest_highway)))

coef_i76 <- round(
  summary(
    lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway, 
       data = prop500 %>% 
         filter(grepl("-76", closest_highway)))

coef_i95 <- round(
  summary(
    lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway, 
       data = prop500 %>% 
         filter(grepl("95", closest_highway)))
    )$coefficients[2,1], 3) # *** p < 0.001

coef_i676 <- round(
  summary(
    lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway, 
       data = prop500 %>%
         filter(grepl("676", closest_highway)))
    )$coefficients[2,1], 3) # not statistically significant, p = 0.0693

```

The scatter plot below shows the relationship between distance to highway and property price along with the regression coefficients for each highway. We observe that without controlling for anything else, property prices generally increase (albeit by very little) are associated with moving away from a highway which agrees with our literature review of highway effects on property prices. 

When predicting property price, the beta coefficient for log distance to highway is `r coef_i676`, `r coef_i76`, and `r coef_us1` for [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"}, and [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"}, respectively (note that the though the beta coefficients were significant with p < 0.01 for [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"} and [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"}, this coefficient was not statistically significant for [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} with a p = 0.069).

```{r prop500_predtable}
# models
lm_us1 <- lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway,
             data = prop500 %>% 
               filter(grepl("US", closest_highway)))

lm_i76 <- lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway,
             data = prop500 %>% 
               filter(grepl("-76", closest_highway)))

lm_i95 <- lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway,
             data = prop500 %>% 
               filter(grepl("95", closest_highway)))

lm_676 <- lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway,
             data = prop500 %>% 
               filter(grepl("676", closest_highway)))

distances <- seq(50, 250, by = 50)

# model predictions
pred_us1 <- exp(predict(lm_us1, newdata = data.frame(log_dist_to_closest_highway = log(distances))))

pred_i76 <- exp(predict(lm_i76, newdata = data.frame(log_dist_to_closest_highway = log(distances))))

pred_i95 <- exp(predict(lm_i95, newdata = data.frame(log_dist_to_closest_highway = log(distances))))

pred_676 <- exp(predict(lm_676, newdata = data.frame(log_dist_to_closest_highway = log(distances))))

# get predicted price changes from philly scale analysis
prop500_pred_table <- data.frame(
  Analysis_Scale = "Philadelphia",
  Distance_m = distances,
  US1_Prices = round(pred_us1),
  I76_Prices = round(pred_i76),
  I95_Prices = round(pred_i95),
  I676_Prices = round(pred_676),
  Chng_US1_Prices = round(pred_us1 - pred_us1[1]),
  Chng_I76_Prices = round(pred_i76 - pred_i76[1]),
  Chng_I95_Prices = round(pred_i95 - pred_i95[1]),
  Chng_I676_Prices = round(pred_676 - pred_676[1]),
  PercChng_US1_Prices = round(100*(pred_us1 - pred_us1[1])/pred_us1[1], 1),
  PercChng_I76_Prices = round(100*(pred_i76 - pred_i76[1])/pred_i76[1], 1),
  PercChng_I95_Prices = round(100*(pred_i95 - pred_i95[1])/pred_i95[1], 1),
  PercChng_I676_Prices = round(100*(pred_676 - pred_676[1])/pred_676[1], 1)
)

```
  

For every 1% increase in distance from [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_i676 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, this means that if a property that is 50m away from the highway, we can expect a similar property a block (100m) further from the highway to be about **`r paste0("$", substr(prop500_pred_table$Chng_I676_Prices[3], 1, 2), ",", substr(prop500_pred_table$Chng_I676_Prices[3], 3, 5))` more expensive** (or a `r prop500_pred_table$PercChng_I676_Prices[3]`% change). For every 1% increase in distance from [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_i76 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`, with a **`r paste0("$", substr(prop500_pred_table$Chng_I76_Prices[3], 1, 2), ",", substr(prop500_pred_table$Chng_I76_Prices[3], 3, 5))` increase** (`r prop500_pred_table$PercChng_I76_Prices[3]` % change) associated with a similar property that is a block further from the highway. For every 1% increase in distance from [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_us1 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`. A price increase of **`r paste0("$", substr(prop500_pred_table$Chng_US1_Prices[3], 1, 1), ",", substr(prop500_pred_table$Chng_US1_Prices[3], 2, 4))`** (`r prop500_pred_table$PercChng_US1_Prices[3]`%) is associated with moving a block further away from  the highway.

The exception here is for properties within 500m of [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"}, where the beta coefficient for log distance to highway is `r coef_i95` (p < 0.001). For every 1% increase in distance from [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"}, property price decreases by `r paste0(round(abs(1.01^coef_i95 - 1), 4)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, a decrease of **`r paste0("$", substr(abs(prop500_pred_table$Chng_I95_Prices[3]), 1, 2), ",", substr(abs(prop500_pred_table$Chng_I95_Prices[3]), 3, 5))`** (`r prop500_pred_table$PercChng_I95_Prices[3]`%) in price is associated with moving a block further away from  the highway. 

We suspect that other factors, such as location preference on the East side of the city are interfering with the expected highway effect. Neighborhoods like Old City, Queen’s Village, and Fishtown are home to many high-income Philadelphians who may have access to amenities that diminish the nuisance of a nearby highway. 

This is our first inkling that **highway effects might not be as strong** as we expected them to be. We now zoom into our **study area** to further understand highway effects in our region of interest.


### Study Region Scale Analysis

#### I-676 Effects

One of OTIS's key interests is the effect of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} on property prices nearby.  Here, we construct a relatively **simple linear model** with a few key predictors to look at the effect of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} on property prices while accounting for some control variables such as the square footage of the property, number of bathrooms, year built, zoning, and zip code among others.

For these analyses, we look at properties **within our study area**.

```{r i676effects_setup_studyareanew, quiet = TRUE, results = 'hide'}
# working with the newest philly_properties dataset where data was cleaned for our studyarea
property_studyarea_new <- st_read("Dataset/property/property_CT_FE.geojson") #1528 rows

# add features for simple linear regression
props_i676_tomodel <- property_studyarea_new %>% 
  # filter() %>% # there are a couple properties with total area < 100; reduces dataset to 990 properties
  # some feature engineering
  mutate(residential = ifelse(category_code_description %in% c("APARTMENTS  > 4 UNITS",
                                                               "MIXED USE",
                                                               "MULTI FAMILY",
                                                               "SINGLE FAMILY",
                                                               "GARAGE - RESIDENTIAL"),
                              1, 0), # is this property residential? (including mixed)
         
         building_code_description_new = case_when(
           grepl("FITNESS CENTER|GOV'T MUNICIPAL/STATE/FEDERAL", building_code_description_new) ~ "MostExpensive",
           grepl("LIFE CARE FACILITY-ASSTD LVNG|CORRECTIONAL|MEDICAL OFFICE BLDNG|PARKING GARAGE/DECK|BOARDING/ROOMING HOSUE|MIXED - RES/COMM|SCHOOL|BANK|OFFICE BLDNG - Mid Rise|DET MIXED-COM/RES-BLT AS COM", building_code_description_new) ~ "MoreExpensive",
           grepl("RETAIL - * SINGLE OCCUPANCY|ROW MIXED-COM/RES-BLT AS COM|ROW MODERN|APARTMENTS - LOW RISE|HOTEL - HI RISE|OFFICE BLDNG - Low Rise|FUNERAL HOME|RESTAURANT|DOWNTOWN ROW TYPE-* SNGL OCCP|WAREHOUSE|TWIN CONTEMPORARY|CAR WASH - AUTOMATIC|RETAIL CONDO|MANUFACTURING/PROCESSING|LOFT (INDUSTRIAL)|APARTMENTS - MID RISE|RELIGIOUS", building_code_description_new) ~ "Average",
           .default = "LeastExpensive" 
           ),
         building_code_description_new = factor(building_code_description_new),
      
         # all the other variables have been cleaned and feature engineered
) %>% 
  select(   # only keep vars necessary for model
    adj_sale_price,
    log_price, distance_to_I676, log_dist_highway,
    residential, 
    year_built, year_built_group,
    central_air, garage_spaces,
    number_of_bathrooms, number_of_bedrooms, total_area,
    exterior_condition, interior_condition, quality_grade,
    building_code_description_new, zoning_group,
    zip_code,
    I676_NS
  )

```

```{r RMSE_calculator}
getRMSE <- function(model_results) {
  # residual sum of squares
  rss <- c(crossprod(model_results$residuals))
  # Mean squared error:
  mse <- rss / length(model_results$residuals)
  # Root MSE:
  RMSE <- sqrt(mse)
  
  return(RMSE)
}

```

Below is a scatter plot showing the relationship between log-transformed distance to [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} and log-transformed property price.

```{r i676effects_plot_studyareanew}
# model with just distance to highway
model_i676 <- lm(log_price ~ log_dist_highway,
                 data = props_i676_tomodel)
# log_dist_highway  0.11110
# Multiple R-squared:  0.01228,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.01163

model_i676_summary <- summary(model_i676)
model_i676_RMSE <- getRMSE(model_i676)

# create a clean table to show model results
model_i676_table <- data.frame(model_i676_summary$coefficients) %>% 
  rename(p = `Pr...t..`) %>% 
  select(Estimate, p) %>% 
  mutate(Estimate = round(Estimate, 3),
         p = round(p, 3))
row.names(model_i676_table) <- c("Intercept", "Log Dist. to I-676")

model_i676_scatter <- 
  ggplot(data = props_i676_tomodel, 
       aes(x = log_dist_highway, y = log_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .2, size = 0.3, show.legend = F,
             color = "#7fe3d6") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", size = 1.2, show.legend = F,
              color = "#7fe3d6", fill = "#7fe3d6") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste(model_i676_table$Estimate[2]),
                x = 5.25,
                y = 14.25),
            color = "#7fe3d6",
            show.legend = F) +
  labs(title = "Property Price (log) as a function of Distance to I-676 (log)",
       subtitle = "Properties in Study Area",
       x = "Log Distance to I-676",
       y = "Log Property Price") +
  theme_minimal()

model_i676_scatter

```

```{r i676_predtable}
distances <- seq(50, 250, by = 50)

# model predictions

# this complicated model needs more parameters
# where possible, i use the median value, otherwise the most common value for these other control variables
pred_i676_more <- exp(predict(model_i676_more, 
                              newdata = data.frame(
                                log_dist_highway = log(distances),
                                residential = 1,
                                building_code_description_new = "LeastExpensive",
                                zoning_group = "CMX(3,4)",
                                year_built_group = "Pre-War",
                                central_air = "Unknown",
                                number_of_bedrooms = "0",
                                number_of_bathrooms = "0",
                                total_area = 0,
                                quality_grade = "Below Average",
                                zip_code = "19107")
                              ))

# get predicted price changes from philly scale analysis
i676_pred_table <- data.frame(
  Analysis_Scale = "I-676 Effects in Study Area",
  Distance_m = distances,
  HighwayOnly_Prices = round(pred_i676_simple),
  HighwayPlus_Prices = round(pred_i676_more),
  Chng_HighwayOnly_Prices = round(pred_i676_simple - pred_i676_simple[1]),
  Chng_HighwayPlus_Prices = round(pred_i676_more - pred_i676_more[1]),
  PercChng_HighwayOnly_Prices = round(100*(pred_i676_simple - pred_i676_simple[1]) / pred_i676_simple[1], 1),
  PercChng_HighwayPlus_Prices = round(100*(pred_i676_more - pred_i676_more[1]) / pred_i676_more[1], 1)
)

# i676_pred_table %>% 
#   kbl(align = "c",
#       caption = "Regression Predictions for I-676 Effects",
#       col.names = c("Analysis Scale", "Distance (m)", "Highway Only Prices", "Highway Plus Prices", "Change Highway Only Prices", "Change Highway Plus Prices", "% Change Highway Only Prices", "% Change Highway Plus Prices")) %>% 
#   kable_styling() %>% 
#   kable_classic(full_width = F, html_font = "Cambria") %>% 
#   row_spec(c(1,3), bold = T, background = "#7fe3d6")

```

From an overly simple model, just looking at how logged distance to [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} predicts logged property price, we see that for properties within 500m of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, distance from the highway does not have a large effect on property price. We see that for every 1% increase in distance to the highway, **we can associate a property price increase of `r paste0(round(1.01^model_i676_table$Estimate[2] - 1, 4)*100,"%")`**. In more understandable terms, this means that for a property that is 50m away from the highway, we can expect a similar property a block further from the highway to be about **`r paste0("$", substr(i676_pred_table$Chng_HighwayOnly_Prices[3], 1, 2), ",", substr(i676_pred_table$Chng_HighwayOnly_Prices[3], 3, 5))` more expensive** (`r i676_pred_table$PercChng_HighwayOnly_Prices[3]`% change). The R-squared value of the model is very low at `r round(model_i676_summary$r.squared, 3)` and the RMSE is very high `r round(model_i676_RMSE,3)`, meaning the model is terrible.

```{r i676effects_model_more2}
model_i676_more_summary <- summary(model_i676_more)
model_i676_more_RMSE <- getRMSE(model_i676_more)
# log_dist_highway                             0.101134640
# Multiple R-squared:  0.3585,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.3421

# create a clean table to show model results
model_i676_more_table <- data.frame(model_i676_more_summary$coefficients) %>% 
  rename(p = `Pr...t..`) %>% 
  select(Estimate, p) %>% 
  mutate(Estimate = round(Estimate, 3),
         p = round(p, 3))
row.names(model_i676_more_table) <- c("Intercept", "Log Dist. to I-676", "Residential", "Building Code - Least Exp.", "Building Code - More Exp.", "Building Code - Most Exp.", "Zoning - CMX3, 4", "Zoning - CMX5", "Zoning - ICMX", "Zoning - IRMX", "Zoning - Other", "Zoning - RM", "Zoning - RMX3", "Zoning - RSA5", "Year Built - New", "Year Built - Post-War Mid", "Year Built - Pre-War", "Year Built - Unknown", "Central Air - Unknown", "Central Air - Yes", "1 Bedrooms", "2 Bedrooms", "3 Bedrooms", "4 Bedrooms", "5 Bedrooms", "Unknown Num. Bedrooms", "1 Bathrooms", "2 Bathrooms", "3-5 Bathrooms", "6 Bathrooms", "7 Bathrooms", "Unknown Num. Bathrooms", "Total Area", "Quality Grade - Below Average", "Quality Grade - Good", "ZIP code - 19106", "ZIP code - 19107", "ZIP code - 19123", "ZIP code - 19130")

model_i676_more_table %>% 
  kbl(align = c("l", rep("c", 2)),
      caption = "Regression Results: Log Price ~ Log Distance to I-676 and Other Predictors",
      col.names = c("Estimate", "p value")) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  kable_classic(full_width = F, html_font = "Cambria") %>%
  row_spec(2, bold = T, background = "#7fe3d6") %>% 
  add_footnote(label = paste0("Adj. R-squared: ", round(model_i676_more_summary$adj.r.squared, 3), ", RMSE: ", round(model_i676_more_RMSE, 3)),
               notation = "none") %>%
  scroll_box(height = "350px") 

```

Finally, we look at a more robust model (which is still relatively simple, including only internal features of the property in addition to ZIP code and logged distance to [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}). This model includes the following predictors: year_built_group (categorical), quality_grade (categorical), number_of_bathrooms (categorical), number_of_bedrooms (categorical), total_area (continuous), central_air (categorical), building_code (categorical), zoning group (categorical), and a variable dictating whether the property is residential or not (binary). This more complex model does a better job at explaining the variance in property price than our previous two models, but is not optimal either. The **adjusted R-squared** for this model is **`r round(model_i676_more_summary$adj.r.squared, 3)`** and our **RMSE** is **`r round(model_i676_more_RMSE, 3)`**. 

When keeping all other predictors constant, the **effect of logged distance to [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} decreases** but remains statistically significant (beta coefficient of `r model_i676_more_table$Estimate[2]`). This means that a 1% increase in distance from the highway is associated with a property price increase of `r paste0(round(abs(1.01^model_i676_more_table$Estimate[2] - 1), 4)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, this means that if a property that is 50m away from the highway, would be about **`r paste0("$", substr(i676_pred_table$Chng_HighwayPlus_Prices[3], 1, 2), ",", substr(i676_pred_table$Chng_HighwayPlus_Prices[3], 3, 5))` more expensive** (`r i676_pred_table$PercChng_HighwayPlus_Prices[3]`% change).

#### Discontinuity Effects

To complicate things even more, within our study area, we see that proximity to [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} has **different effects** on the [North (Callowhill)]{style="color: #eb5600;"} and [South (Chinatown)]{style="color: #1a9988;"} sides.

```{r discontinuity_data, quiet = TRUE, results = 'hide'}
# with most recently updated data (990 properties)
discontinuity_plot_ungrouped <- props_i676_tomodel %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(distance_to_I676m = distance_to_I676 * 0.3048,
         distance_to_highway = case_when(
           I676_NS == "north" ~ distance_to_I676m,
           I676_NS == "south" ~ -distance_to_I676m
           ))

discontinuity_plot <- discontinuity_plot_ungrouped%>% 
  group_by(distance_to_highway, I676_NS) %>%
  summarise(mean_log_price = mean(log_price, na.rm = T), .groups = "drop")

# median property prices on each side
med_north <- round(median(discontinuity_plot_ungrouped %>% 
                      filter(I676_NS == "north") %>% 
                      pull(adj_sale_price)))

med_south <- round(median(discontinuity_plot_ungrouped %>% 
                      filter(I676_NS == "south") %>% 
                      pull(adj_sale_price)))

# range of property prices on each side
range_north <- round(range(discontinuity_plot_ungrouped %>% 
                      filter(I676_NS == "north") %>% 
                      pull(adj_sale_price)))

range_south <- round(range(discontinuity_plot_ungrouped %>% 
                      filter(I676_NS == "south") %>% 
                      pull(adj_sale_price)))

```

```{r disc_predtable}
# models (redoing them because i want to use log_dist_highway)
i676_north <- lm(log_price ~ log_dist_highway,
                 data = discontinuity_plot_ungrouped %>% 
                   filter(I676_NS == "north"))

i676_south <- lm(log_price ~ abs(log_dist_highway),
                 data = discontinuity_plot_ungrouped %>% 
                   filter(I676_NS == "south"))

distances <- seq(50, 250, by = 50)

# model predictions
pred_i676_n <- exp(predict(i676_north, newdata = data.frame(log_dist_highway = log(distances))))

pred_i676_s <- exp(predict(i676_south, newdata = data.frame(log_dist_highway = log(distances))))

# get predicted price changes from philly scale analysis
i676NS_pred_table <- data.frame(
  Analysis_Scale = "I-676 Effects -- North/South",
  Distance_m = distances,
  North_Prices = round(pred_i676_n),
  South_Prices = round(pred_i676_s),
  Chng_North_Prices = round(pred_i676_n - pred_i676_n[1]),
  Chng_South_Prices = round(pred_i676_s - pred_i676_s[1]),
  PercChng_North_Prices = round(100*(pred_i676_n - pred_i676_n[1]) / pred_i676_n[1], 1),
  PercChng_South_Prices = round(100*(pred_i676_s - pred_i676_s[1]) / pred_i676_s[1], 1)
)

#       caption = "Regression Predictions for I-676 Effects -- North/South",
#       col.names = c("Analysis Scale", "Distance (m)", "North of I-676 Prices", "South of I-676 Prices", "Change North of I-676 Prices", "Change South of I-676 Prices", "% Change North of I-676 Prices", "% Change South of I-676 Prices")) %>% 
#   kable_styling() %>% 
#   kable_classic(full_width = F, html_font = "Cambria") %>% 
#   row_spec(c(1,3), bold = T, background = "#7fe3d6")

```

In the plot above, we see that on the [North side]{style="color: #eb5600;"} of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, property prices remain relatively stable and unaffected by distance to the highway. The median property price in the [North]{style="color: #eb5600;"} is `r paste0("$", substr(med_north, 1, 3), ",", substr(med_north, 4, 6))`. When predicting logged property price, the beta coefficient for distance to highway is `r coef_north`, meaning the **highway has no effect on the price** (`r paste0("$", substr(i676NS_pred_table$Chng_North_Prices[3], 1, 1), ",", substr(i676NS_pred_table$Chng_North_Prices[3], 2, 4))` increase when moving an additional block north from the highway, starting at 50m away, `r i676NS_pred_table$PercChng_North_Prices[3]`% change).

On the other hand, in the [South side]{style="color: #1a9988;"} of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, property prices are within the same range of prices as in the [North side]{style="color: #eb5600;"}, but the median property price is slightly higher at `r paste0("$", substr(med_south, 1, 3), ",", substr(med_south, 4, 6))`. 

When predicting logged property price to the [South]{style="color: #1a9988;"} of the highway, the beta coefficient for distance to highway is `r coef_south`, meaning **distance to highway has a very small, positive effect on the price**. For every 1m increase in distance from [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(exp(coef_south)-1, 3)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, our simple model predicts that a property 150m away from [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} would be **`r paste0("$", substr(i676NS_pred_table$Chng_South_Prices[3], 1, 2), ",", substr(i676NS_pred_table$Chng_South_Prices[3], 3, 5))` more expensive** (`r i676NS_pred_table$PercChng_South_Prices[3]` % change) compared to a property 50m away from the expressway.

This demonstrates that in our study area, increased **distance to the highway is associated with an increase in property price** that is only really seen on the [South side]{style="color: #1a9988;"} of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}.

## Study of Highway Caps in Other Cities

Three completed highway capping projects in the United States were selectively included here as case studies and guideline for constructing our alternatives in the context of the Chinatown Stitch. These sites either share similar traits with the Chinatown Stitch or possess dramatically different parameters of both the surrounding neighborhood and the project itself. 

### Klyde Warren Park

This project **connected** the predominantly Black Uptown neighborhood with the arts district and Downtown while also providing a community gathering space with free programming year-round. Since its opening in 2012, the park has **enhanced the land value** in the surrounding area, creating a positive economic impact on the City of Dallas including faster office and multifamily construction growth. However, it brought up concerns of **"green gentrification"** which benefits the interests of developers over displaced communities.

![Klyde Warren Park - image and info from https://www.klydewarrenpark.org/](Final%20R%20Markdown/Images/KlydeWarrenPark.png)

+ **City:** Dallas, TX
+ **Completion date:** 2013
+ **Area Covered:** 5.4 acres (235,000 sqft)
+ **Cost:** $112 million
+ **Type of project:** Park/Open Space


### Cap at Union Station

The project addressed the **40-year scar** that was created by the construction of the inner-belt highway (I-670) by **reconnecting the Columbus downtown area and the Short North neighborhood**. The cap acts as a bridge for through traffic across I-670 while also providing leasable spaces to many retail shops and restaurants, ultimately providing an **inviting urban streetscape**.

![Cap at Union Park - image from https://www.crexi.com/properties/1653293/ohio-the-cap-at-union-station](Final%20R%20Markdown/Images/CapUnionStation.png)

+ **City:** Columbus, OH
+ **Completion date:** 2004
+ **Area Covered:** 25,500 sqft
+ **Cost:** $7.8 million
+ **Type of project:** Commercial


### The Big Dig at the Central Artery

Creating more than 300 acres of open land with **over 45 parks and public plazas**, the Big Dig project replaced the deteriorating I-93 (Central Artery) with an underground expressway that links downtown Boston to the Boston Logan airport. This project also improved the North End and Waterfront neighborhoods’ access to downtown Boston and **reduced traffic congestion**, providing ~$168 million per year in time and cost savings.

![Central Artery - image from https://themindcircle.com/boston-big-dig/](Final%20R%20Markdown/Images/CentralArtery.png)

+ **City**: Boston, MA
+ **Completion date:** 2007
+ **Area Covered:** 2,350 acres
+ **Cost**: $14.8 billion
+ **Type of project:** Mixed Use

#### Summary of Highway Cap Impacts

A common thread across the impacts of caps in other cities is **neighborhood access and connection as well as increased value of land**. The Chinatown Stitch will not only reconnect Chinatown North to Chinatown, but also provide much needed open, green space for the community. A potential challenge after the construction of the Chinatown Stitch will be balancing the positive effects of higher land value and the **activation of commercial and residential opportunities** with **affordability and cultural preservation of the character** of Philadelphia's Chinatown.

## Feature Engineering

<h4>**Feature List**</h4>

<h5><span style="color: #1a9988;"><b>Continuous Variables</b></span></h5>
1. `distance_to_highway`: Distance to the nearest segment of I-676.  
2. `distance_to_city_hall`: Euclidean distance to Philadelphia City Hall. Used as a proxy for centrality and access to core amenities.  
3. `distance_to_nearest_transit`: Distance to the closest metro or trolley station.  
4. `distance_to_nearest_school`: Distance to the nearest public school.  
5. `distance_to_nearest_hospital`: Distance to the closest hospital.  
6. `distance_to_nearest_bikelane`: Distance to the closest designated bike route.  
7. `nearest_restaurant_dist_m`: Distance to the nearest restaurant.  
8. `distance_to_nearest_park`: Distance to the nearest public park. Used as a proxy for environmental quality and recreational access; relevant for scenario planning.  
9. `distance_to_nearest_water`: Distance to nearest river or water body.  
10. `year_built`: Construction year of the property.  
11. `crime_nn5`: Distance to the 5 nearest crime incidents.  
12. `total_livable_area`: Total usable interior square footage.  
13. `number_of_bathrooms`: Total number of bathrooms.  
14. `number_of_bedrooms`: Total number of bedrooms.  

<h5><span style="color: #eb5600;"><b>Categorical Variables</b></span></h5>
1. `exterior_condition`: Condition rating of building exterior.  
2. `interior_condition`: Condition rating of building interior.  
3. `LPSS_PER1000`: Number of low-produce supply stores per 1,000 people.  
4. `general_construction`: Broad classification of building construction type.  
5. `garage_spaces`: Number of on-site parking spaces.  
6. `quality_grade`: Overall quality classification.  
7. `separate_utilities`: Indicator of utility separation across units.  
8. `central_air`: Binary indicator for presence of central air conditioning.  
9. `nhoods_name`: Assigned neighborhood name.  
10. `zoning`: Official land use designation per city zoning code.  
11. `category_code`: Land use code. Used as a secondary classification of use beyond zoning.  
12. `landuse`: Land use classification. Complements zoning by reflecting actual built function.  
13. `zip_code`: ZIP code of the parcel. Used as a proxy for unobserved neighborhood-level effects.   

<h4>**Feature Exploration**</h4>
<h5><b>Correlation Matrix</b></h5>
We examined correlations between continuous variables and sale price. This analysis aimed to identify variables with strong predictive relevance and assess potential multicollinearity. **Total Livable Area** shows the strongest positive correlation with **sale price**, reaffirming its role as a key structural determinant of property value. **Number of bedrooms** and **bathrooms** also exhibit moderate positive associations.  

Among spatial accessibility variables, **sale price** is positively correlated with **distance to I-676** as discussed before extensively, supporting the assumption of highway-induced disamenity. Distances to **City Hall**, **transit**, and **water bodies** show weak but directionally consistent relationships.  

Importantly, **distance to park** shows relatively low correlation with price but is retained due to its direct policy relevance—Scenario 1 includes the construction of a cap park, making this variable critical for evaluating environmental improvements. **Crime Rate (crime_nn5)** is moderately negatively correlated with sale price, indicating that public safety remains a consistent influence on market value.  

Notably, distance to **bikelanes** and **transit** are highly correlated (r ≈ 0.6), as are distance to **hospital** and **City Hall**. A negative correlation is also observed between distance to **schools** and **water**, indicating potential spatial segregation.

```{r correlation matrix, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE,fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}

colnames(cor_matrix) <- var_labels[colnames(cor_matrix)]
rownames(cor_matrix) <- var_labels[rownames(cor_matrix)]

corrplot(
```

<h5>Engineered Features</h5>
We engineered a series of features to better capture structural, spatial, and policy-relevant characteristics of each parcel by `Imputation`, <code>Log Transformation</code>, <code>Reclassification</code>.

<span style="color: #1a9988;"><b>1. Imputation and Discretization</b></span><br>
Maintaining observation count is critical, especially with our small sample sizes (1529 observations) and spatially heterogeneous data. To avoid data loss and ensure model stability, we applied simple imputation and discretization strategies for several variables.  

<code>Core structural variables</code>: Impute median values for number of bedrooms and bathrooms and then discretize into categorical groups. Invalid or missing values in total livable area were set to zero to retain observations and maintain feature consistency.  
<code>Parcel depth</code>: Impute mean value for missing values.

<span style="color: #1a9988;"><b>2. Log Transformation</b></span><br>
To address right-skewed distributions and improve model performance, we applied log transformation to key continuous variables:  
<code>adj_sale_price</code> (DV), <code>total livable area</code>, and all <code>distance-related variables</code> (e.g. distance to highway, City Hall, water, parks, etc.).  

This transformation compresses extreme values, enhances linearity, and reduces heteroscedasticity, making the data more suitable for regression-based modeling. The effect is shown for total livable area, where the log-transformed version approximates a normal distribution.

```{r Log Transofrmed - Distribution of Total Livable Area ,fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
plot_df <- property_final %>%
  mutate(
    total_livable_area_log = log1p(total_livable_area) 
  )

plot1 <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = total_livable_area)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#1B8370", alpha = 0.8) +

        x = "Total Livable Area",

    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5)
  )

plot2 <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = total_livable_area_log)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#1B8370", alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Log-transformed Total Livable Area",
        x = "(Log) Total Livable Area", 
        y = "Count")  +
  xlim(5, 9) +  
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),

  )
combined_plot <- plot1 + plot2 +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1)) +
  plot_annotation(

#    caption = "Figure X.X",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16,face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
      plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
    )
  )
combined_plot
```

<span style="color: #1a9988;"><b>3. Reclassification</b></span><br>
Several categorical variables contain fragmented or inconsistent codes, making them hard to interpret and statistically unstable. We reclassified the following features into fewer, more meaningful categories to improve interpretability and model robustness.  

<code>Land Use</code>: Reclassified into four categories—open space/business, commercial, civic-residential, and high-density residential—to reflect broader functional distinctions relevant to highway impacts and planning interventions. This allows for better alignment between land use types and potential zoning change responses.  

<code>Year Built</code>: Transformed into categorical groups (Pre-War, Post-War Mid, Modern, New, Unknown) to reflect periods of construction and building age, which often correspond to differences in structural standards and renovation likelihood.  

<code>Quality-related variables</code>: Reclassify (<i>interior/exterior condition</i>, <i>quality grade</i>) into ordinal categories (Good / Average / Below Average) to retain the interpretive meaning of subjective assessments.  

<code>Central air and garage availability</code>: Reclassify these variables into new categorical factors, with missingness flags constructed to preserve data integrity.  

<code>Zoning</code>: Zoning is a key institutional variable in both the modeling and scenario components of this study. Given the large number of detailed zoning codes in the raw dataset, we constructed a simplified variable <code>zoning_group</code> to improve interpretability and support policy simulation.  

<ul>
  <li><b>CMX(1,2,2.5) - Neighborhood Commercial</b>: Includes CMX1, CMX2, CMX2.5; represents low-density, local-serving commercial districts.</li>
  <li><b>CMX(3,4) - Community Commercial</b>: Includes CMX3 and CMX4; mid-scale commercial corridors serving wider areas.</li>
  <li><b>CMX5 - Center City Commercial</b>: High development intensity and location in center city.</li>
  <li><b>RM / RMX – Residential</b>: Includes RM1, RM2, RM4, and RMX3, including medium- to high-density housing districts.</li>
  <li><b>RSA5 - Residential</b>: Residential Single-Family Attached Districts as low-density housing.</li>
  <li><b>IRMX – Industrial Residential Mixed-Use</b>: A mix of low-impact industrial, artisan industrial, residential, and neighborhood commercial uses.</li>
  <li><b>ICMX – Industrial Commercial</b>: Represents industrial-commercial zones with low land-use flexibility and limited market responsiveness.</li>
  <li><b>I2/SPPOA</b>: “I2” and “SPPOA” were excluded from the analysis due to their extremely small sample sizes, which are insufficient to support reliable model training and testing.</li>
</ul>
    

```{r FE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, quiet=TRUE, results='hide'}
median_bedroom <- median(as.numeric(as.character(property_final$number_of_bedrooms)), na.rm = TRUE)
median_bathroom <- median(as.numeric(as.character(property_final$number_of_bathrooms)), na.rm = TRUE)

property_CT <- property_final %>%
  filter(!zoning %in% c("I2", "SPPOA"))%>%
    mutate(category_code_chain = case_when(
    category_code == '1 ' ~ "1:Single Family",
    category_code == '10' ~ "10:Offices",
    category_code == '12' ~ "12:Vacant Land - Non-residential",
    category_code == '14' ~ "14:Apartments > 4 units",
    category_code == '15' ~ "15:Retail",
    category_code == '16' ~ "16:NA",
    category_code == '2 ' ~ "2:Multi Family",
    category_code == '3 ' ~ "3:Mixed Use",
    category_code == '4 ' ~ "4:Commercial",
    category_code == '5 ' ~ "5:Industrial",
    category_code == '6 ' ~ "6:Vacant Land",
    category_code == '7 ' ~ "7:Garage - Commercial",
    category_code == '8 ' ~ "8:Garage - Residential",
    category_code == '9 ' ~ "9:Hotel",
  ))%>%
  mutate(
    # Land Use
    landuse = case_when(
      landuse %in% c("Park/Open Space", "Other/Unknown", "Commercial Business/Professional") ~ "Open Space/Business",
      landuse %in% c("Commercial Consumer", "Commercial Mixed Residential",
                     "Industrial", "Transportation", "Culture/Amusement") ~ "Commercial",
      landuse %in% c("Civic/Institution", "Residential High") ~ "Residential High/Civic",
      TRUE ~ landuse
    ),

    # Year Built
    year_built = as.numeric(year_built),
#    year_built_missing = ifelse(is.na(year_built), 1, 0),
    
    year_built_group = case_when(
      is.na(year_built) ~ "Unknown",
      year_built < 1940 ~ "Pre-War",
      year_built < 2000 ~ "Post-War Mid",
      year_built < 2020 ~ "Modern",
      year_built >= 2020 ~ "New"
    ),
    year_built_group = factor(year_built_group, levels = c("Pre-War", "Post-War Mid", "Modern", "New", "Unknown")),

    # Log Transforms
    log_price = log(adj_sale_price),
    log_dist_highway = log(distance_to_I676 + 1),

    # Central Air
    central_air = case_when(
      central_air %in% c("Y", "1")  ~ "Y",
      central_air %in% c("N", "0") ~ "N",
      TRUE ~ "Unknown"
    ),
    central_air = factor(central_air),
#    central_air_missing = ifelse(central_air == "Unknown", 1, 0),

    # Garage Spaces
#    garage_spaces_missing = ifelse(is.na(garage_spaces), 1, 0),
    garage_spaces = case_when(
#      is.na(garage_spaces) ~ "Unknown",
      garage_spaces == 0 | garage_spaces == 1 ~ "less than 2",
      TRUE ~ "2 or more"
    ),
    garage_spaces = factor(garage_spaces),

    # Bedrooms
    number_of_bedrooms = as.numeric(as.character(number_of_bedrooms)),
    number_of_bedrooms_missing = ifelse(is.na(number_of_bedrooms), 1, 0),
    number_of_bedrooms_filled = ifelse(is.na(number_of_bedrooms), median_bedroom, number_of_bedrooms),
    number_of_bedrooms = case_when(
      is.na(number_of_bedrooms) ~ "Unknown",
      number_of_bedrooms == 0 ~ "0",
      number_of_bedrooms == 1 ~ "1",
      number_of_bedrooms %in% c(2, 3) ~ "2",
      number_of_bedrooms %in% c(5, 6) ~ "3",
      number_of_bedrooms == 4 ~"4",
      number_of_bedrooms %in% c(7, 9, 12) ~ "5"
    ),
    number_of_bedrooms = factor(number_of_bedrooms),

    # Bathrooms
    number_of_bathrooms = as.numeric(as.character(number_of_bathrooms)),
    number_of_bathrooms_missing = ifelse(is.na(number_of_bathrooms), 1, 0),
    number_of_bathrooms_filled = ifelse(is.na(number_of_bathrooms), median_bathroom, number_of_bathrooms),
    number_of_bathrooms = case_when(
      number_of_bathrooms == 0 ~ "0",
      number_of_bathrooms == 1 ~ "1",
      number_of_bathrooms == 2 ~ "2",
      number_of_bathrooms %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ "3-5",
      number_of_bathrooms == 6 ~ "6",
      number_of_bathrooms == 7 ~ "7",
      TRUE ~ "Unknown"
    ),
    number_of_bathrooms = factor(number_of_bathrooms),

    # Total Livable Area
    total_livable_area = ifelse(is.na(total_livable_area) | total_livable_area == 1, 0, total_livable_area),

    # Quality Grade
    quality_grade = case_when(
      quality_grade %in% c("A ", "A-") | is.na(quality_grade) ~ "Good",
      quality_grade %in% c("3 ", "C+", "C")  ~ "Average",
      TRUE ~ "Below Average"
    ),
    quality_grade = factor(quality_grade, levels = c("Good", "Average", "Below Average")),
    quality_grade_missing = ifelse(is.na(quality_grade), 1, 0),

    # Construction
    general_construction = as.character(general_construction),
    general_construction = case_when(
      is.na(general_construction) ~ "Unknown",
      TRUE ~ general_construction
    ),
    general_construction = factor(general_construction),
    general_construction_missing = ifelse(general_construction == "Unknown", 1, 0),

    # Separate Utilities
    separate_utilities = case_when(
      is.na(separate_utilities) ~ "Unknown",
      TRUE ~ separate_utilities
    ),
    separate_utilities = factor(separate_utilities, levels = c("A", "B", "C", "Unknown")),
    separate_utilities_missing = ifelse(separate_utilities == "Unknown", 1, 0),

    # Exterior Condition
    exterior_condition = case_when(
      exterior_condition == 2 | is.na(exterior_condition)~ "Average",
      exterior_condition %in% c(1, 6, 7)  ~ "Good",
      exterior_condition %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ "Below Average"
 #     TRUE ~ "Unknown"
    ),
    exterior_condition = factor(exterior_condition),

    # Interior Condition
    interior_condition = case_when(
      interior_condition %in% c(1,6) ~ "Good",
      is.na(interior_condition) | interior_condition %in% c(2, 5, 7) ~ "Average",
      interior_condition %in% c(3, 4, 5, 6) ~ "Below Average",
      TRUE ~ "Unknown"
    ),
    interior_condition = factor(interior_condition),

    # Category Code
    category_code_original = as.character(category_code),
    category_code_group = case_when(
      category_code == "12" ~ "6 ",
      category_code == "14" ~ "2 ",
      category_code == "10" ~ "4 ",
      category_code == "15" ~ "5 ",
      category_code == "16" ~ "4 ",
      category_code == "7 "  ~ "4 ",
      category_code == "8 "  ~ "6 ",
      category_code == "9 "  ~ "3 ",
      category_code %in% c("1 ", "2 ", "3 ", "4 ", "5 ", "6 ") ~ category_code,
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    category_code = factor(category_code_group),

    # Zoning
    zoning_group = case_when(
      zoning %in% c("CMX5") ~ "CMX5",
      zoning %in% c("IRMX") ~ "IRMX",
      zoning %in% c("RM1", "RM2", "RM4") ~ "RM",
      zoning %in% c("RMX3") ~ "RMX3",
      zoning %in% c("RSA5") ~ "RSA5",
      zoning %in% c("ICMX") ~ "ICMX",
 #     zoning %in% c("SPPOA") ~ "SPPOA",
 #     zoning %in% c("I2") ~ "I2",
      zoning %in% c("CMX2.5", "CMX2", "CMX1") ~ "CMX(1,2,2.5)",
      zoning %in% c("CMX3", "CMX4") ~ "CMX(3,4)",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    zoning_group = factor(zoning_group),

    zoning = case_when(
      is.na(zoning) ~ "Unknown",
      TRUE ~ zoning
    ),
    zoning = factor(zoning),
    zip_code = factor(zip_code)
  )
```

**3. Comparing north and south – Continuous Variable**  

The relationship between `log sale price` and `log(distance to City Hall)` differs spatially across I-676. On the <span style="color: #1a9988;">**south side**</span>, encompassing neighborhoods such as Center City East, Chinatown, Old City, and Logan Square, there is a clear negative relationship — as distance from City Hall increases, sale prices decrease. This suggests a strong centrality premium tied to proximity to Philadelphia’s civic and economic core.  

In contrast, the <span style="color: #eb5600;">**north side**</span>, including Callowhill and West Poplar, shows a much weaker and slightly positive relationship. This may reflect less concentrated commercial development or weaker integration with the downtown core. Although both sides are within short distances of City Hall, the intensity of urban functions, transit connectivity, and historic development patterns differ, potentially driving the spatial discontinuity in the price response to centrality in the south side.  

The relationship between `log sale price` and `log(distance to I-676)` is positive on the <span style="color: #1a9988;">**south side**</span>. As properties are located farther from the highway, their sale prices increase. This pattern suggests the presence of a localized disamenity effect, where proximity to I-676 lowers residential property values.  

On the <span style="color: #eb5600;">**north side**</span>, no significant relationship is observed; distance to the highway does not appear to influence sale price in this area. The spatial contrast indicates that the impact of highway proximity is not uniform and is conditioned by local context.  

The relationship between `log sale price` and `log-transformed total livable area` shows a strong and linear positive correlation on both sides. However, there is a stronger correlation on the <span style="color: #1a9988;">**south side**</span>, indicating that an increase in livable area leads to a greater increase in sale price compared to the north.  

This difference suggests higher price sensitivity to internal space in southern neighborhoods, which may be linked to market demand for larger units or the scarcity of spacious housing stock. On the <span style="color: #eb5600;">**north side**</span>, while the relationship is also positive, the weaker correlation implies that additional square footage adds less marginal value to properties in that area.

**4. Comparing north and south – Categorical Variables**  

For `zoning` variable, notably, zoning groups such as CMX5 (high-density commercial) and RM (multi-family residential) have slightly higher average prices on the <span style="color: #1a9988;">**south side**</span>, which aligns with their proximity to Center City and concentration of commercial amenities.  

The only exception is CMX(3,4), Community Commercial Mixed-Use, where the <span style="color: #eb5600;">**north side**</span> shows a marginally higher average sale price. Overall, properties on the <span style="color: #1a9988;">**south side**</span> of I-676 command higher sale prices across zoning types, reflecting stronger market demand, superior locational access, and more intensive land use.  

Even under the same zoning designations, the <span style="color: #eb5600;">**north side**</span> shows relatively weaker market performance, suggesting structural differences in development intensity, accessibility, and perceived land value between the two sides.  

For `quality_grade` variable, across all three grades—Good, Average, and Below Average, the <span style="color: #1a9988;">**south side**</span> consistently exhibits higher average sale prices than the <span style="color: #eb5600;">**north side**</span>.  

The gap is particularly pronounced for properties rated as Good, where the <span style="color: #1a9988;">**south side**</span> outperforms the <span style="color: #eb5600;">**north side**</span> by a notable margin. This suggests that structural quality contributes more significantly to price variation on the <span style="color: #1a9988;">**south side**</span>, likely due to stronger buyer expectations and market demand in neighborhoods closer to Center City.  

In contrast, the <span style="color: #eb5600;">**north side**</span> shows a flatter price gradient across quality levels, implying that quality improvements translate into smaller price increases. This may reflect a more price-constrained or supply-driven market where building quality plays a relatively limited role in shaping property sale price.

# Modeling
## OLS Modeling  
The model achieves an R-squared of 0.45, indicating that approximately 45% of the variation in log-transformed sale prices is explained by the included predictors. The adjusted R-squared is 0.450, which adjusts for the number of predictors and confirms that the model has moderate explanatory power. The RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) is 0.506, meaning the average deviation between the predicted and actual log sale prices is about 0.51. Given the complexity of housing markets and the limited sample size (N = 1528), this level of accuracy is acceptable for baseline modeling and policy scenario evaluation.  

### Most Powerful Predictors

Among the variables, several variables stand out as statistically significant and substantively important, and will serve as core inputs in our future predictive models.  

1. `Distance to I-676` shows a positive and highly significant effect, the coefficient is 0.154, supporting the disamenity hypothesis and serving as a focal variable for the Stitch impact.  
2. `Total livable area` and `interior condition` are strong structural predictors of housing value.  
3. `Distance to parks, City Hall, and water bodies` all have negative coefficients, indicating that closer access to amenities increases price, aligning with urban economic theory.  
4. `Crime proximity` (distance to five nearest incidents) has a negative, significant effect on price, consistent with safety-related price penalties.  
5. `Zoning group`, `land use`, and `neighborhood` function as spatial fixed effects, capturing regulatory and locational differences not explained by numeric features.  

In addition to these core variables, we retain several features that are currently insignificant but important for capturing variation under different scenarios.  

1. `Exterior condition` and `quality grade`, might affect price more strongly in subsets of the data or under scenario changes.  
2. `General construction`, `garage availability`, and `separate utilities`, which reflect the physical configuration of properties.  
3. `Year built group`, though not always significant, encodes historical development phases.  
4. `LPSS_PER1000` (low produce supply stores per 1,000 people) captures potential food access inequities and will be relevant under future zoning or community health-focused scenarios.  
5. `Number of bedrooms` and `Number of bathrooms` show weaker effects once size is controlled for, but are retained for interpretability and flexibility in downstream scenario design.  
6. `log_nearest_restaurant_dist_m` and `log_nearest_grocery_dist_m` are not statistically significant in the current model. This may suggest that in our study area—where most parcels are in walkable, amenity-rich neighborhoods like Center City and Chinatown—variation in food access is low, and therefore has limited power in explaining price differences. However, these variables are conceptually important and may gain significance in future scenario modeling, especially if the Stitch project leads to shifts in retail landscape or perceived accessibility. For that reason, we retain them in the feature set.  

### Multicollinearity

To address potential multicollinearity, we conducted a **Generalized Variance Inflation Factor (GVIF)** analysis [@GVIFpaper]. Most variables showed acceptable VIF values below 5. Only `garage_spaces` presented a high Variance Inflation Factor or VIF (6.95), likely due to its overlap with other structural variables. We retained it due to its policy relevance—for example, its role in parking regulations, transit-oriented development, and future scenario simulation related to land use and accessibility.  

In addition, we identified that `zip_code` and `nhoods_name` are highly collinear. Certain neighborhoods are almost fully nested within specific ZIP codes, making the two variables statistically redundant. To avoid aliasing and ensure model stability, we removed `zip_code` and retained `nhoods_name` to capture neighborhood-level fixed effects.  

Altogether, this comprehensive feature set reflects both current explanatory power and anticipated value for scenario modeling. The next stage will use this full variable group as input for machine learning models (`RF`, `XGBoost`,`RL`) to enable robust spatial prediction under different futures.

## Predictive Modeling
Built on our simple OLS model, we train **four models** based on Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Regularized Linear Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost respectively for property price predictions:

+ **Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)** is a basic linear model that captures simple relationships but struggles with messy or complex data.

+ **Regularized Linear Regression (RLS)** improves on OLS by adding penalties to reduce overfitting, making it useful for datasets with many or irrelevant variables.

+ **Random Forest (RF)** averages many decision trees built on different data slices, handling complex patterns well but with less interpretability.

+ **XGBoost (XGB)** builds trees sequentially, each learning from the last’s errors, excelling in accuracy for structured data tasks.

After training and validation, the Random Forest model achieved the best performance among the tested models, with **a MAPE of 34.02% and a MAE of $214,118**, indicating a moderate level of accuracy, with average prediction errors of approximately one-third of actual prices. **The model performs particularly well for properties priced around $400,000 and demonstrates strong reliability for scenario-based forecasting in zoning categories such as RMX3, CMX3, and CMX4**. In contrast, its higher error rates in industrial zones and high-rise commercial areas (e.g., CMX5 and IRMX) reflect the more volatile and site-specific nature of property values in those markets, which may involve complex redevelopment potential or specialized land uses not fully captured by the model.

### Data Preparation

Based on feature engineering results, we select the 23 most relevant features plus geographical location (longitude and latitude) as independent variables, and use log-transformed property price as the dependent variable. To build and evaluate our model, we split the dataset into two parts: **70%** as the training set to fit the model, and **30%** as the test set to evaluate its accuracy.

### Model Training

Within the training set, we use **spatial cross-validation**, which tests the model on different areas to avoid overfitting to nearby properties. **K-means Clustering** is used when creating the cross-validation folds. This helps prevent the model from "cheating" by seeing similar areas in both training and testing.

#### Workflow

Each model is trained following a workflow, including defining, tuning, and evaluating. Here, we'd like to take **Random Forest workflow** as an example.

 1. `rf_plan` defines the Random Forest model structure. A Random Forest is a collection of many decision trees. Each tree looks at the data differently, and their combined result gives a more accurate and stable prediction.
 
 2. `rf_grid` is a grid of possible settings (combinations of `mtry` and `min_n`) used for tuning the random forest model. The `mtry` parameter controls how many predictors are randomly selected at each split in a tree, affecting model diversity and performance. The `min_n` parameter sets the minimum number of observations required to split a node, influencing tree depth and overfitting. By **evaluating different combinations of these hyperparameters**, the model can identify the configuration that yields the best predictive performance.
 
 3. `rf_wf` is a workflow that connects our preprocessing (`model_rec`) and model (`rf_plan`) together. It ensures that all the data is cleaned the same way every time we train or test the model.
 
 4. `rf_tuned` trains many Random Forest models using the different settings from `rf_grid`, and tests each one using our **spatial cross-validation folds**. This is the "try everything and see what works best" step. Each fold helps estimate how well the model will generalize.
 
 5. `rf_best_params` picks the best settings from the tuning process based on which combination gave the **lowest RMSE**. Then `rf_best_wf` finalizes the workflow with the best-performing parameters locked in.
 
 6. `rf_val_fit_geo` finally train the finalized Random Forest on the entire training set and test its accuracy on the test set. This gives the most realistic estimate of how well the model will perform on new, unseen property data.


```{r model_specifications, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Moedl Specifications
lm_plan <- 
  linear_reg() %>% 
  set_engine("lm")

glmnet_plan <- 
  linear_reg() %>% 
  set_args(penalty  = tune()) %>%
  set_args(mixture  = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet")

rf_plan <- rand_forest() %>%
  set_args(mtry  = tune()) %>%
  set_args(min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_args(trees = 1000) %>% # 3000 
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") %>% 
  set_mode("regression")

XGB_plan <- boost_tree() %>%
  set_args(mtry  = tune()) %>%
  set_args(min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_args(trees = 100) %>% # smaller
  set_engine("xgboost") %>% 
  set_mode("regression")

# Hyperparameter grid

glmnet_grid <- expand.grid(penalty = seq(0, 1, by = .25), 
                           mixture = seq(0,1,0.25))
rf_grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2,5,10,13,30,45), 
                       min_n = c(50,100,150,200,250)) # 50-250
xgb_grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2,5,10,13,30,45), 
                       min_n = c(50,100,150,200,250)) # same as rf

# create workflow
lm_wf <-
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(model_rec) %>% 
  add_model(lm_plan)
glmnet_wf <-
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(model_rec) %>% 
  add_model(glmnet_plan)
rf_wf <-
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(model_rec) %>% 
  add_model(rf_plan)
xgb_wf <-
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(model_rec) %>% 
  add_model(XGB_plan)

# Spatial CV approach
property_train_sf <- st_as_sf(property_train, coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326)
property_train_sf <- property_train_sf %>%
  mutate(
    Longitude = st_coordinates(.)[, 1],
    Latitude = st_coordinates(.)[, 2]
  )
set.seed(123)
cv_splits_zoning <- group_vfold_cv(property_train,
                                group = "zoning_group")
set.seed(123)
cv_splits_cluster <- spatial_clustering_cv(
  property_train_sf,
  v = 20,
  cluster_function = "kmeans"
)

cv_splits_geo <- cv_splits_cluster
control <- control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
metrics <- metric_set(yardstick::rmse, yardstick::rsq, yardstick::mape, yardstick::smape)
```
